title: Final exam — 40 questions across all modules
body_md:
## The capstone written exam

You've worked through eight modules of theory, examples, and practice. This exam asks you to apply that knowledge under timed conditions. The format:

- **40 multiple-choice questions**, five per module, drawn from the patterns we covered.
- **Pass mark: 80%** (32 correct). Below that, you'll see what you missed and can retake the exam.
- **Honest mode.** No retry within a single question — pick once and the answer is submitted. The exam is for *you*; cheating yourself defeats the purpose.
- **Pass once and your result is recorded** for the certificate page.

Take your time. There's no clock other than the one you set yourself.

questions.question: Why are highly personalised scam messages now economical to send to millions of people?

choices.text: Spam filters got weaker.
Phishing-as-a-Service and breach data collapsed the cost per attempt to cents.
choices.explanation: Industrialised supply chain — kits, hosting, leads, cash-out — drives cost down, not click-through up.

choices.text: Users click more than they used to.
Fraud was decriminalised in major countries.

questions.question: Which channel has the highest open rate but the lowest preview information for a link?

choices.text: Email
SMS
choices.explanation: Texts have a >95% open rate in minutes and no built-in link preview, which is why smishing is so effective.

choices.text: Voice call
Web ad

questions.question: A six-week WhatsApp friendship that ends with an 'investment opportunity' is the calling card of which actor type?

choices.text: Opportunist
Nation-state operation
Organized fraud ring running pig-butchering
choices.explanation: Long-rapport scripts targeting strangers are the trademark of commercial fraud rings, not nation-state actors.

choices.text: Disgruntled insider

questions.question: Which term best fits an attacker impersonating a CFO to redirect a wire transfer to a new bank account?

choices.text: Ransomware
BEC (Business Email Compromise)
choices.explanation: BEC is the umbrella for executive-impersonation schemes that redirect payments.

choices.text: Quishing
Credential stuffing

questions.question: How would you stop a multi-participant deepfake video meeting from succeeding?

choices.text: Train yourself to spot artifacts on faces in the call.
Require a call-back to a known number on a different channel before any large transfer.
choices.explanation: Out-of-band verification on a channel the attacker can't control is the only durable defence against AI-augmented impersonation.

choices.text: Move all approvals into encrypted email.
Add a written PIN inside the same email thread.

questions.question: 'Only 3 spots left — closes in 12 hours' stacks which two Cialdini principles?

choices.text: Authority + Reciprocity
Social Proof + Authority
Scarcity + Commitment
Scarcity + Liking (via being 'specially chosen')
choices.explanation: A countdown is scarcity; the framing 'you've been selected' triggers liking through flattery.

questions.question: How do you break a pretext in a suspicious call?

choices.text: Demand the caller's badge number.
Hang up and call back on a number you already had.
choices.explanation: The pretext lives inside the channel; switching channels collapses it.

choices.text: Argue with the caller until they slip up.
Stay on the line so police can trace it.

questions.question: A vishing call asks you to stay on the line while you transfer money to a 'safe account'. What is the *strongest* single tell?

choices.text: The caller has a foreign accent.
The caller insists on staying on the line during a financial action.
choices.explanation: Legitimate fraud teams never coach you through a transfer in real time. That's diagnostic.

choices.text: The caller knows the last four digits of your card.
The call came outside business hours.

questions.question: A stranger you've chatted with for weeks introduces a small crypto platform and helps you make a successful test withdrawal. The strongest indicator of pig-butchering is:

choices.text: The promised returns are unrealistic.
The introduction came sideways from a stranger who built rapport for weeks.
choices.explanation: Real investments are not introduced by strangers via DM. The pipeline is the diagnostic, not the returns.

choices.text: A relative of theirs supposedly works at the platform.
They suggest starting small.

questions.question: Which phrase in a live call is sufficient on its own to end the conversation?

choices.text: 'For security, please install AnyDesk so I can clean your computer remotely.'
choices.explanation: No legitimate vendor uses remote-access tools over cold calls. This is the universal tech-support fraud signature.

choices.text: 'I'll send you the details by email.'
'Could you confirm your name?'
'Sorry for the noise on my side.'

questions.question: In the URL `https://login.paypal.com.account-verify.io/signin`, what is the registered domain?

choices.text: paypal.com
login.paypal.com
account-verify.io
choices.explanation: The registered domain is the two labels immediately before the first slash. Everything to the left is a label the attacker chose.

choices.text: signin.io

questions.question: Which character substitution is the most common lookalike-domain trick?

choices.text: Capital 'I' for lowercase 'l'
Cyrillic 'а' for Latin 'a'
choices.explanation: Homoglyph substitution from Cyrillic to Latin produces visually identical domains; Punycode (`xn--…`) is what reveals them in some browsers.

choices.text: Digit '8' for 'B'
Underscore inserted in random places

questions.question: Your password manager refuses to auto-fill on what looks like your bank's login page. What is most likely happening?

choices.text: The manager's vault is corrupted.
The domain doesn't match your saved entry — likely a phishing site.
choices.explanation: A no-autofill is one of the most reliable phishing detectors. Trust it.

choices.text: The bank changed its login flow without telling anyone.
The page is in incognito mode.

questions.question: What's the right next move when you spot a clear phishing email at work?

choices.text: Reply 'this is a scam' to the sender.
Click the 'Report phishing' button in your mail client and forward the email as an attachment to security; move to junk.
choices.explanation: One-click report + as-attachment forward preserves headers and triggers company-wide blocking within minutes.

choices.text: Forward to everyone on the team so they can learn from it.
Delete it immediately to be safe.

questions.question: A poster next to the office copier displays a QR code and says 'Your Microsoft 365 password is expiring — scan to renew'. What's the safest move?

choices.text: Scan and renew — IT often posts these.
Renew through the company's official SSO portal that you already use, and report the poster to IT.
choices.explanation: Posted QR codes are not the right channel for credential changes — anyone with badge-in access could have put them up. Use the trusted SSO portal you already use, and warn IT.

choices.text: Ignore it — passwords don't expire anymore.
Scan only if the URL preview looks plausible.

questions.question: Your password leaks in a breach of a small forum. The single most urgent action is:

choices.text: Change the password on the forum.
Change the password on the bank, email, and any other site where the same password was reused.
choices.explanation: The risk is credential stuffing across other services. Bank and email are highest-value.

choices.text: Create a new email and migrate everything.
Wait to see if your bank notifies you.

questions.question: Which MFA tier is phishing-resistant by protocol design?

choices.text: SMS one-time codes
TOTP authenticator app
Hardware key / passkey (FIDO2)
choices.explanation: FIDO2 binds the signature to the origin URL — a fake page cannot produce a valid signature for the real domain.

choices.text: Email-link confirmation

questions.question: Where does a passkey actually live, in terms of where it gets synced?

choices.text: On the server of the site you log into.
Inside your platform account (iCloud Keychain, Google account, or password manager).
choices.explanation: That's why securing your platform account matters: it now holds your passkeys.

choices.text: Printed in your browser's settings.
In a public registry.

questions.question: Your work email uses TOTP for MFA, but recovery is still via SMS to a number you'll leave behind for six months abroad. What's the right move before you travel?

choices.text: Leave it — TOTP already covers the risk.
Disable SMS recovery and add a hardware key or trusted-device backup; set a port-out PIN with your carrier.
choices.explanation: SMS recovery is bypass-able via SIM-swap; TOTP doesn't help if the recovery flow itself accepts SMS.

choices.text: Move your number to a friend's phone.
Switch to email-only recovery.

questions.question: What is the single most-leveraged item in a yearly credential audit?

choices.text: Renaming your accounts to less guessable usernames.
Rotating passwords flagged as weak / reused / breach-known by your password manager's health report.
choices.explanation: The manager already does the audit — your job is to act on the flagged entries from highest-value down.

choices.text: Deleting all old emails.
Adding a CAPTCHA to your home Wi-Fi.

questions.question: An online store wants to charge you for a PS5 at 90% off MSRP via Bitcoin or gift cards, on a 14-day-old domain. Which signal is the *strongest* by itself?

choices.text: The domain age of 14 days.
Payment options exclude major cards and use only non-reversible methods.
choices.explanation: No legitimate retailer goes crypto/gift-card-only — the irreversibility is the entire point of the scam.

choices.text: The 'only 3 left' urgency.
The store name contains 'sony'.

questions.question: After being scammed publicly, you get a DM from a 'forensic recovery specialist' offering to retrieve your crypto for a 20% fee in USDT. The strongest single tell that this is a follow-up scam is:

choices.text: The fee is high.
They contacted you proactively after seeing your public report.
choices.explanation: Real recovery firms don't cold-DM victims. The unsolicited contact is the pattern.

choices.text: They want payment in USDT.
Their screenshots look polished.

questions.question: A 'CFO' emails accounts payable asking to update a vendor's IBAN before the next invoice. Which control prevents the wire-redirection fraud?

choices.text: Verify the From-domain matches the vendor's real domain.
Call the vendor's CFO on a phone number you already had and verbally confirm the IBAN change.
choices.explanation: BEC often runs from genuinely compromised mailboxes; only an out-of-band callback breaks it.

choices.text: Forward to IT for analysis before processing.
Check the IBAN format is country-valid.

questions.question: Which payment-method combination defends best against both physical and digital card skimming?

choices.text: Memorising your number.
Apple Pay / Google Pay where possible + virtual cards + real-time transaction alerts.
choices.explanation: Tap-to-pay tokenises the number so the merchant never sees it. Virtual cards limit damage where tap isn't supported. Alerts give you minutes to react.

choices.text: Only shopping on stores you've never used before.
Avoiding online shopping entirely.

questions.question: You realise you sent a $30K wire based on a BEC email last night. What's the *first* action that gives the best recovery odds?

choices.text: Email the bank requesting a recall.
Call the bank's fraud line and request an urgent SWIFT wire recall.
choices.explanation: Recall odds collapse with time, and only phone moves at minute resolution.

choices.text: File a police report first to get a case number.
Engage a Telegram 'recovery service'.

questions.question: Which defensive strategy is *most durable* against improving generative-AI capabilities?

choices.text: Training to spot visual deepfake artifacts.
Out-of-band verification protocols (callback to known numbers, family code words).
choices.explanation: Process defences are independent of model capability.

choices.text: Avoiding any AI-generated content entirely.
Trusting AI-text detector tools.

questions.question: Your 'daughter' calls in tears asking for $4K bail in gift cards and begs you not to tell anyone. What's the right move?

choices.text: Buy the gift cards immediately.
Ask for the family code word; if she can't say it, hang up and call her directly.
choices.explanation: Code words survive voice cloning. Gift-card bail is not a real legal mechanism anywhere.

choices.text: Ask 'put me on with the officer'.
Tell her you'll wire instead.

questions.question: Mid-call, your CFO plus two other execs ask you on Zoom to wire $200K in 30 minutes. Which control would actually defeat a deepfake here?

choices.text: Inspect for facial artifacts in real time.
After the call, message the CFO on company Slack from your contacts list and ask written confirmation.
choices.explanation: The deepfake lives inside the meeting; a different channel breaks it.

choices.text: Ask the CFO for a piece of internal trivia.
Process the wire — three execs is overwhelming.

questions.question: What's the single most reliable check on whether an unexpected message from an old college friend is really her?

choices.text: Run the email through an AI-text detector.
Ask about a specific shared memory that isn't in any public profile.
choices.explanation: AI impersonators have your friend's public info; they don't have private shared history.

choices.text: Reply 'are you really my friend?'
Send the money 'just in case'.

questions.question: Which combination of checks best evaluates whether a viral political video is genuine?

choices.text: Inspect the politician's facial movements.
Find the clip on the politician's verified channels or established news outlets; cross-reference reverse-search; check Content Credentials.
choices.explanation: Multiple provenance signals beat any single artifact-detection approach.

choices.text: Trust the source if the account has many followers.
Use an automated deepfake detector and trust its result.

questions.question: A 'Free Flashlight + Compass' app from a third-party store wants microphone, contacts, SMS, and Accessibility access. The biggest red flag is:

choices.text: Microphone access alone.
All of these — and especially Accessibility, which gives full remote-control-style power.
choices.explanation: Accessibility is the most dangerous permission for an arbitrary app; combined with the rest, this is a textbook malware profile.

choices.text: The app being on a third-party store.
The app having a 'Free' label.

questions.question: Your phone suddenly shows 'No service' while other people's phones on the same carrier work. What's the right first move?

choices.text: Drive to the carrier store to fix the SIM.
Borrow a phone, call the carrier's fraud line to freeze the SIM transfer, then sign into email and bank from a computer.
choices.explanation: SIM-swap is a race. The longer the attacker holds your number, the more accounts they can drain.

choices.text: Wait an hour to see if it's just a carrier outage.
Restart your phone repeatedly.

questions.question: A browser extension you want asks for 'Read and change data on all websites'. The right approach is:

choices.text: Grant it immediately — that's how extensions work.
Verify the publisher first; if legitimate, accept but disable the extension in incognito and confine it to a single profile.
choices.explanation: The permission is unavoidable for some extensions, but the blast radius can be scoped.

choices.text: Refuse and install a different extension that doesn't need it.
Install as a temporary trial.

questions.question: In a café you need to log into your bank. The strongest practical security posture is:

choices.text: Connect to a paid VPN before logging in.
Use the bank's mobile app on cellular data instead of the laptop on Wi-Fi.
choices.explanation: Removes you from the café's network entirely and uses an app with certificate pinning.

choices.text: Tether to a friend's hotspot.
Trust HTTPS — modern banks are safe over any network.

questions.question: To protect everyone in your household (kids, older relatives, IoT) from accidentally connecting to phishing domains, the highest-leverage setup is:

choices.text: Install antivirus on every device.
Configure your router to use a filtering DNS provider (NextDNS, Cloudflare for Families, Quad9).
choices.explanation: One router setting protects every device, automatically, with no per-device maintenance.

choices.text: Give each family member a paid VPN.
Tell everyone to be careful what they click.

questions.question: Three password-reset emails arrive for sites you don't use, plus a 'login from Lagos' alert, plus a new mail-forwarding rule. What's the strongest evidence the account is compromised?

choices.text: The login from Lagos.
The unfamiliar auto-forwarding rule — it's the diagnostic action of an account takeover.
choices.explanation: Forwarding rules silently siphon mail and are one of the highest-confidence indicators of email-account compromise.

choices.text: The number of reset emails.
All three together aren't really proof.

questions.question: You see a 'login from Singapore' alert and can't sign back in — password just changed. Your phone is on the kitchen counter. First action?

choices.text: Try the reset from your phone.
Grab a known-clean device, open incognito, reset the email from there.
choices.explanation: Clean-device rule avoids any compromise on the phone itself and prevents attacker software watching.

choices.text: Call email-provider customer support.
Wait a few minutes to see what happens.

questions.question: An attacker is actively in your inbox right now. As an individual (not an organisation), what should you do?

choices.text: Quietly screenshot what they do for evidence.
Sign out all sessions, change the password, then capture the activity log.
choices.explanation: Contain first. The activity log is preserved after eviction; the marginal evidence from watching isn't worth the active risk.

choices.text: Reply to one of their emails to confirm their identity.
Set up DevTools monitoring on the inbox.

questions.question: Someone opened a fraudulent credit card in your name (US). First-day actions:

choices.text: Call the issuer of the fraudulent card to close it.
Freeze all three credit bureaus, file IC3/FTC, file local police, dispute with the issuer.
choices.explanation: Bureau freezes prevent further accounts opening; federal reports feed aggregate investigations; local police gives you a case number.

choices.text: Wait for your credit report to update first.
Post about it on social media to warn friends.

questions.question: Three months after a credential-stuffing incident on your email, the single most useful follow-up action is:

choices.text: Create a new email and migrate everything.
Re-audit the email's security settings: active sessions, forwarding rules, OAuth apps, recovery contacts, login history.
choices.explanation: Attackers leave delayed-action footholds that are silent for months. Re-audit catches them.

choices.text: Buy identity-theft insurance.
Reinstall the OS on all your devices.
